This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: moving spoken dialogue systems beyond half-duplex, turn-based interaction toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex behavior with overlaps, backchannels, and latency-aware turn-taking. The central idea is to adapt an autoregressive LLM into a wall-clock-synchronous dialogue model by interleaving two speaker streams in fixed-duration chunks, inserting periodic synchronization tokens, and training the model to predict deduplicated speech-unit sequences. The paper further proposes a three-stage training recipe that relies heavily on synthetic spoken dialogue derived from text corpora, followed by relatively limited real dual-channel dialogue fine-tuning. Empirically, the authors report substantial gains over dGSLM in semantic meaningfulness while maintaining comparable naturalness, and they also simulate interaction under one-chunk latency.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, ambitious, and potentially impactful. The problem formulation is compelling, and the paper makes a serious attempt to bridge a real gap between current speech/LLM systems and human conversational dynamics. The strongest aspect of the work is conceptual: the authors identify that “full duplex” is not just a matter of streaming ASR/TTS, but of synchronizing generation with time and modeling both channels jointly. The proposed chunked interleaving format with periodic synchronization markers is simple, elegant, and plausibly extensible. The latency-tolerant interaction mechanism, where the model predicts the user’s current chunk before generating its own next chunk, is also a thoughtful design choice that directly addresses deployment constraints rather than assuming oracle access to the interlocutor’s hidden state.

The empirical story is also promising. The reported gains in meaningfulness over dGSLM are large, both in automatic evaluation via ASR-transcribed perplexity and in human MOS. The out-of-distribution results on CANDOR are especially encouraging, since they support the claim that leveraging text-pretrained LLM knowledge plus synthetic speech data improves semantic generalization beyond what speech-only dialogue models achieve. The human evaluation suggests that the proposed method closes much of the semantic gap to re-synthesized ground truth while preserving turn-taking naturalness at roughly the same level as the baseline. If these findings are robust, they would represent a meaningful advance.

That said, I also have several substantial concerns, mostly around evaluation validity, ablation completeness, and the degree to which the experiments support the strongest claims in the paper.

The first major concern is that the paper’s central claim is about full-duplex dialogue agents, but the evaluation remains somewhat indirect. Much of the evidence comes from continuation-mode generation, where the model generates both sides of the conversation. This is useful, but it is not the same as evaluating an interactive agent responding to real user speech online. Even the “interaction” experiments are simulated via LLM-LLM interaction, not human-agent interaction, and the user side is generated by another model rather than coming from real humans. This leaves open whether the system actually behaves well in realistic online settings with ASR errors, speaker variability, disfluencies, unexpected interruptions, and non-cooperative timing. The paper is careful in places, but the title and framing suggest a stronger demonstration of deployed full-duplex interaction than is actually shown.

Relatedly, the latency-tolerance claim is only partially validated. The model is trained to anticipate the missing current user chunk and is said to tolerate Internet-scale latencies up to 240 ms, but the experiments appear to simulate one-chunk latency under chunk sizes of 160/200/240 ms. This is a reasonable first step, but it does not fully characterize robustness to variable latency, jitter, packet loss, or ASR/tokenization delay. In practice, end-to-end latency in a cloud speech system includes audio capture, encoding, transmission, tokenization, model inference, and vocoding. The paper motivates this issue well, but the experimental setup abstracts away many of these components. I would have liked to see a more explicit accounting of end-to-end latency budgets and a clearer distinction between “one-chunk delayed token access” and actual deployed latency.

A second major concern is the reliance on ASR-transcribed text perplexity as the primary semantic automatic metric. This metric is understandable given the difficulty of evaluating spoken dialogue semantics directly, but it introduces several confounds. First, ASR errors may distort the generated content differently across systems. Second, the transcriptions explicitly ignore overlapping speech, which is a core phenomenon the paper aims to model. Third, perplexity under a text dialogue model is at best a proxy for coherence or appropriateness, and may reward generic continuations. The human meaningfulness MOS helps mitigate this concern, but the automatic semantic evaluation should be interpreted cautiously. It would strengthen the paper to include additional semantic metrics or analyses, such as response relevance judged by humans, transcript-based pairwise preference, or task-specific dialogue consistency measures.

The naturalness evaluation also raises questions. The turn-taking metrics are based on correlations between average event durations in generated continuations and ground-truth continuations conditioned on the same prompt. This follows prior work, but it is still a fairly weak proxy for conversational naturalness. Matching average pause or overlap statistics does not necessarily imply locally appropriate turn-taking behavior. A model could achieve decent correlation while placing overlaps or backchannels at pragmatically odd moments. The human naturalness MOS is therefore important, but the reported naturalness scores are all clustered closely together, and the differences between systems are small. This makes it difficult to assess whether the proposed synchronization mechanism truly improves interactive timing quality, or whether the main gains are semantic while timing remains roughly baseline-level.

A third concern is that the paper bundles together several innovations, but the ablation evidence is limited. The method includes at least four distinct ingredients: initialization from a text-pretrained LLM, synthetic speech pretraining from text dialogue, the chunked interleaved synchronous format with periodic speaker tags, deduplication plus interpolation, and the latency-tolerant user-chunk prediction mechanism. The current experiments mainly compare the full system against dGSLM and vary chunk size. This does not isolate which components matter most. For example, how much of the semantic gain comes simply from using Llama3 plus synthetic dialogue speech, independent of the synchronous formulation? How important is deduplication relative to raw HuBERT sequences? Does the periodic synchronization token materially outperform alternative positional/time encodings? Does stage 2 help beyond stage 1 plus stage 3? Does predicting the user’s missing chunk improve interaction quality relative to simply waiting or using stale context? These are central scientific questions, and the paper would be much stronger with targeted ablations.

The deduplication/interpolation design is clever, but it also seems under-validated. The authors argue that duplicate HuBERT tokens reduce semantic density and that periodic synchronization tokens preserve coarse timing. However, the interpolation heuristic at synthesis time is quite crude: when multiple deduplicated tokens occur in a chunk, each is repeated equally to fill the chunk. This may distort durations and prosody in ways that are not captured by the current evaluations. The paper states that the effect is imperceptible even at 240 ms chunk size, but this appears anecdotal. Since timing fidelity is central to the contribution, I would expect either objective reconstruction analyses or a focused perceptual study comparing deduplicated/interpolated synthesis against non-deduplicated alternatives.

There are also some fairness and baseline questions. dGSLM is a reasonable prior baseline, but it is also architecturally and training-wise quite different, and perhaps disadvantaged by not leveraging large-scale text pretraining. Since one of the paper’s main claims is that standard autoregressive LLMs can be adapted for synchronous spoken dialogue, a stronger comparison would include more recent speech-text LLM baselines or simpler cascaded systems with streaming policies. For example, how would a strong streaming ASR + text LLM + TTS pipeline with explicit turn-taking heuristics perform on meaningfulness and naturalness? The related work mentions cascaded systems, but the experiments do not compare against one. Without such baselines, it is hard to know whether the gains come from full-duplex joint modeling per se or from simply using a much stronger semantic backbone.

The training data story is interesting but somewhat underspecified. The paper states 212k hours of synthetic spoken dialogue and about 2k hours of real spoken dialogue, but the exact composition of the text datasets, filtering criteria, dialogue domains, and train/test contamination safeguards are not described in enough detail here. Since the semantic gains may depend heavily on the breadth and quality of the synthetic data, reproducibility and interpretation would benefit from more transparency. Similarly, the use of Bark with only 10 speaker presets may limit acoustic diversity; it would be useful to know whether the model overfits to synthetic TTS artifacts and how this affects transfer to real speech.

I also found the human evaluation somewhat limited for a paper making strong claims about conversational interaction. Thirty-two annotators and 180 items is acceptable for an initial study, but each item receives only three ratings, and the evaluation focuses on continuation clips rather than live interaction. The MOS protocol is adapted for meaningfulness and naturalness, but these constructs are broad. In particular, “naturalness” here seems to conflate timing naturalness with speech quality and perhaps overall conversational plausibility. Since the paper acknowledges that the vocoder is relatively simple, it would help to disentangle speech quality from turn-taking quality. A targeted pairwise preference study on overlap placement, backchannel appropriateness, interruption handling, or response timing would better support the full-duplex claims.

Another issue is that the paper’s notion of “full duplex” is still constrained. The model predicts fixed-size chunks and uses one speaker tag per chunk as a synchronization anchor. This is a practical approximation, but it discretizes time coarsely and may not capture finer-grained conversational phenomena. The chunk sizes explored, 160–240 ms, are already close to the scale of human turn-transition gaps. It would be useful to discuss more explicitly what kinds of synchrony this representation can and cannot express. For example, can it model very short acknowledgments, laughter bursts, or rapid interruption onset accurately? The current framing occasionally suggests a more complete solution than the representation may warrant.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the proposed representation is novel and intuitive, and the empirical results suggest that the approach is viable and substantially improves semantic quality over a strong prior spoken-dialogue baseline. I especially appreciate that the paper does not merely add speech tokens to an LLM, but explicitly addresses timing and delayed input. This is a meaningful conceptual contribution. The work also opens a promising direction for integrating conversational dynamics into autoregressive language models without abandoning the benefits of large-scale text pretraining.

For improvement, I would strongly encourage the authors to add or clarify the following. First, provide ablations isolating the contributions of deduplication, synchronization tokens, stage-2 training, and user-chunk prediction under latency. Second, include stronger baselines, ideally a streaming cascaded system and/or a recent speech-text LLM adapted to dialogue. Third, expand the interaction evaluation beyond LLM-LLM simulation, even if only with a small human-agent pilot or replay-based evaluation using real held-out user streams. Fourth, provide more detailed latency accounting and robustness tests under variable delay. Fifth, strengthen the validation of the interpolation heuristic and clarify whether speech quality affects the naturalness judgments. Sixth, improve methodological transparency around synthetic data generation and dataset composition.

In summary, I view this as a strong and timely paper with a compelling idea and promising results, but one whose experimental evidence does not yet fully match the breadth of its claims. The semantic improvements appear convincing; the full-duplex interaction claims are plausible but less conclusively demonstrated. If accepted, the paper would likely stimulate valuable follow-up work on synchronous spoken interaction with LLMs. My overall assessment is positive but not unreserved: this is a meaningful contribution, though it would benefit from stronger ablations and more realistic interactive evaluation to fully substantiate its central claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting an autoregressive text LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can model overlapping speech, backchannels, and latency-tolerant interaction. The core idea is to interleave two speakers’ speech-unit streams with periodic synchronization tokens that encode coarse wall-clock timing, while training on deduplicated HuBERT token sequences to reduce redundancy. To address limited real spoken-dialogue data, the authors use a three-stage training pipeline with large-scale synthetic speech generated from text dialogues, followed by fine-tuning on about 2k hours of real dual-channel dialogue. Empirically, the paper reports substantially better semantic quality than dGSLM, comparable naturalness, some OOD generalization from Fisher to CANDOR, and simulated interaction robustness under one-chunk latency (160–240 ms).
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving from turn-based spoken interfaces to genuinely synchronous/full-duplex dialogue.
The proposed tokenization/formatting scheme is conceptually simple and compatible with standard autoregressive LLMs, making the approach practically appealing.
Strong motivation for incorporating timing and latency explicitly, including a concrete mechanism for one-chunk-ahead prediction under delayed user input.
The three-stage training recipe is well motivated given the scarcity of real spoken-dialogue data and leverages abundant text dialogue corpora effectively.
Empirical results suggest large gains in semantic meaningfulness over the main baseline dGSLM, including in human evaluation.
Includes both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation (Fisher and CANDOR), which is valuable for assessing robustness.
The interaction-mode simulation between two models trained on different datasets is an interesting demonstration of the framework’s flexibility.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is narrow: the main baseline is essentially only dGSLM, while stronger modern speech-text/dialogue baselines or cascaded streaming systems are not evaluated.

The semantic evaluation metric is indirect and potentially fragile: ASR transcription followed by perplexity under a text dialogue model may conflate ASR errors, formatting choices, and language-model preferences rather than directly measuring dialogue quality.

The naturalness metric based on Pearson correlation of average event durations with ground truth is unusual and only weakly tied to perceptual quality; high or low correlation may not reflect realistic turn-taking quality.
The paper’s central claim of full-duplex capability is demonstrated only in simulation (LLM-LLM interaction), not with real human interactive latency experiments.
The interpolation heuristic after deduplication may distort timing/prosody, but its impact is not rigorously quantified beyond anecdotal claims of imperceptibility.
Ablations are limited: the contribution of synchronization tokens, deduplication, synthetic-data stages, chunk size, and user-chunk estimation are not cleanly isolated.
Human evaluation uses only 3 raters per item and relatively small scale, with limited detail on prompt balancing, statistical significance testing between systems, and inter-rater reliability.
The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases such as interruption handling errors, semantic drift during interaction, or pathological overlap behavior.
methodological_flaws: The semantic evaluation pipeline is scientifically weak as a primary measure of dialogue meaning: converting generated speech to text with ASR, discarding overlaps, and then scoring with a text-only dialogue LM introduces multiple uncontrolled sources of error and systematically removes precisely the full-duplex phenomena the paper claims to model.

The naturalness evaluation computes Pearson correlation between average turn-taking event durations in generations and ground-truth continuations conditioned on the same prompt. This does not establish that generated dialogues are natural; it only measures similarity to one continuation distribution and may reward imitation of corpus-specific timing statistics rather than conversational appropriateness.

The interaction setting does not involve real users or real networked deployment. Therefore the claim of robustness to Internet-scale latency is only partially supported; simulation with another model is not equivalent to human-agent interaction under realistic ASR/VAD/network jitter conditions.

The interpolation method assumes equal repetition of deduplicated tokens within a chunk when reconstructing periodic HuBERT sequences. This is a heuristic with no formal justification and could alter acoustic timing in a way that affects both naturalness and downstream evaluation; the paper lacks quantitative validation of reconstruction error.

The comparison to dGSLM may not be fully fair because SyncLLM benefits from massive text-pretrained Llama3 and 212k hours of synthetic TTS dialogue, whereas the baseline is speech-only and older. While this is part of the paper’s contribution, the experimental design does not disentangle architectural advantages from scale/data advantages.

The paper claims that periodic synchronization tokens give the model a sense of time, but there is no formal or empirical verification that the model learns calibrated temporal reasoning beyond chunk indexing. This is more an engineering encoding than evidence of true synchrony modeling.

Several important implementation details needed to assess empirical validity are missing or under-specified, such as decoding strategy, latency budget breakdown including tokenization/vocoder, exact prompt construction, and statistical significance for key comparisons.
